name: runc
vendor: Open Container Initiative (Linux Foundation), donated by Docker

foundation.via: Part of the Open Container Initiative

summary: The reference OCI runtime: a small Linux command-line tool that turns a bundle into a running container, and the default runtime underneath containerd and Docker Engine.
intro: runc does one job: given an OCI bundle, a directory with a root filesystem and a `config.json`, it creates the container the configuration describes and runs its process. It sets up Linux namespaces, cgroups (v1 or v2, directly or through systemd), mounts, capabilities, seccomp filters and AppArmor or SELinux labels, then starts the program and gets out of the way. Its commands follow the OCI Runtime Specification’s lifecycle: `runc create` builds the container without starting the program, `runc start` runs it, and `runc kill`, `runc delete` and `runc state` follow; `runc run` does create and start in one go. It also runs rootless containers as an ordinary user and checkpoints and restores running containers with CRIU. It is written mostly in Go, runs only on Linux, and its own README says it is “a low level tool not designed with an end user in mind”: it does not pull images, set up networks or keep logs.

Those jobs belong to the engines above it. Docker Engine hands containers to containerd, and containerd, the most common runtime behind Kubernetes nodes, uses runc by default through its `io.containerd.runc.v2` shim. CRI-O switched its default to crun, a runtime written in C, in version 1.31 (September 2024), and Podman picks crun first when both are installed. Since runc 1.3 (April 2025) a new minor release comes about every six months, with published end-of-support dates: 1.5.0 arrived in June 2026 and 1.5.2 in September, 1.6.0 is due at the end of October 2026, and support for 1.3 ends the same month. Because every container on a host is started by the same runc binary with host privileges, its security record matters: high-severity container escapes were fixed in 2019, 2021, 2024 and three at once in November 2025, and runc can now be built with libpathrs, a Rust library for safe path handling.
strengths: The reference implementation of the OCI Runtime Specification, and the default runtime in containerd and so in Docker Engine and many Kubernetes nodes: the most widely exercised Linux container runtime
Covers the Linux container feature set: cgroup v2 and the systemd cgroup driver, rootless containers, seccomp, AppArmor and SELinux, and checkpoint/restore with CRIU
Predictable releases since 2025: a minor version about every six months, with published support windows for older branches
Signed releases and an independent security audit by Cure53
limits: Containers share the host kernel and runc runs with host privileges, so a runc or kernel bug can mean an escape; for untrusted code, gVisor or Kata Containers add a second boundary
Only the lowest layer: no image pulling, networking, logging or restart policies, so you almost always use it through containerd, Docker, CRI-O or Podman
Linux only, and written in Go, which the CRI-O maintainers cite when choosing crun for faster starts and lower memory use
Older branches drop off quickly under the six-month cadence: the 1.2 branch and earlier are already unsupported, and 1.3 support ends in October 2026

snippet.title: Run a container with runc alone, from its README (needs root, or `runc spec --rootless`)
source: # fill the root filesystem, here by exporting busybox from Docker
docker export $(docker create busybox) | tar -C rootfs -xvf -
runc spec                 # writes a template config.json for the bundle
runc run mycontainerid    # create + start, attached to the terminal
# or step by step, as an engine does
runc create mycontainerid && runc start mycontainerid
runc kill mycontainerid KILL && runc delete mycontainerid

sections.title: Notable container escapes fixed in runc
sections.intro: All high severity. Each one let code inside a container, or a malicious image, reach the host.

rows.label: CVE-2019-5736
values: A container running as root could overwrite the host’s runc binary through `/proc/self/exe` and gain root on the host; affected runc up to 1.0-rc6 and Docker before 18.09.2

rows.label: CVE-2021-30465
values: Swapping a mount destination for a symlink at the right moment put mounts outside the container’s root filesystem

rows.label: CVE-2024-21626
values: A leaked file descriptor gave a new process a working directory on the host filesystem, through `runc exec` or a malicious image

rows.label: CVE-2025-31133, -52565, -52881
values: Mount races around masked paths and `/dev/console`, and redirected writes to procfs, allowed escapes and denial of service

story: Docker first started containers with LXC. In Docker 0.9, on March 10, 2014, it made its own library the default: libcontainer, a Go library that called the kernel’s container features directly, which the team said “drastically reduces the number of moving parts” and protected Docker from differences between LXC versions and distributions.

On June 22, 2015, when Docker, CoreOS and others announced the Open Container Project, Docker donated a command-line wrapper around libcontainer as runC, with all the “plumbing” Docker used to talk to the kernel, to be the reference implementation of a common runtime standard. libcontainer moved into the runc repository. The first 1.0 release candidate came in June 2016, but runc 1.0.0 only shipped on June 22, 2021, after a long run of release candidates.

Over the same years runc became the layer nearly every Linux container engine called. The CVE-2019-5736 escape in February 2019 showed what that meant: one bug exposed Docker, Kubernetes and other platforms at once. Minor releases stayed irregular (1.1 in January 2022, 1.2 in October 2024) until the maintainers adopted a six-month cadence with published support windows, starting with 1.3 in April 2025.

choices.choice: Call the kernel directly instead of going through LXC
choices.why: LXC behaved differently across versions and distributions. A Go library managing namespaces, cgroups, capabilities and AppArmor itself removed that dependency and the bugs that came with it.

choices.choice: A separate binary started per container
choices.why: Engines start runc to set up a container and let it exit, so the engine can be upgraded or restarted without touching running containers, and any OCI-compatible runtime can replace runc.

choices.choice: Reference implementation of an open specification
choices.why: Donating the runtime to the OCI and tying it to the Runtime Specification let other runtimes, such as crun, youki, gVisor and Kata Containers, accept the same bundles, so engines aren’t bound to one implementation.

timeline.text: Docker 0.9 makes libcontainer its default instead of LXC (March 10)
Docker donates runC to the new Open Container Project (June 22)
CVE-2019-5736: a container can overwrite the host’s runc binary (February)
CRI-O makes crun its default instead of runc (1.31, September)
runc 1.3 starts a six-month release cadence (April); three escapes fixed (November)
